strengths: Addresses a practically useful setting: unlearning updates require only the forgetting data and pretrained model, without retained or surrogate data.
Substantial experimental effort includes three deletion settings, six dataset settings, 15 baselines, multiple architectures, and results reported over five trials.
Class and subclass deletion results are promising: MU-Mis achieves accuracy gaps of 0.07 on CIFAR-100 and 0.20 on CIFAR-20-Sea. Selected experiments also demonstrate substantial runtime savings.

The two-term loss ablation supports combining target and irrelevant-class sensitivities. Sequential deletion experiments and output-distribution comparisons provide useful evidence beyond one-shot accuracy.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is not established. Section III-B drops the training trajectory's dependence on the perturbed sample and the softmax derivative without controlling approximation error. The assertion that the summed cross-sample residual in Eq. (5) is negligible does not follow from ReLU activation and can fail for correlated samples. Moreover, sensitivity to infinitesimal input perturbations is not equivalent to influence under sample deletion.

The privacy evaluation is insufficient for the strong protection claims. The reported MIA metric measures only the fraction of forgotten examples classified as members, without false-positive rates or adequate attack specifications. Lower values need not indicate greater similarity to retraining: on CIFAR-20-Sea, MU-Mis scores 1.25 versus 51.61 for retraining. Calibrated attacks using matched nonmembers and retraining controls are needed; accuracy and whole-dataset average KL cannot establish removal of sample information.

The broad effectiveness claims are contradicted by random-subset results in Table A5. On CIFAR-10, MU-Mis has an average gap of 2.80 versus 0.51 for finetuning and 1.84 for the unchanged pretrained model; test accuracy drops to 91.50 versus 94.75 after retraining. On SVHN, its gap is 2.36 versus 0.47 for SalUn. These limitations directly affect the claimed ability to remove individual sample contributions while preserving utility.

Practical tuning is considerably more involved than the main description suggests. Appendix C-D introduces dynamic loss reweighting with kappa=80 for important experiments, while stopping thresholds range up to 10 in sequential deletion. The robustness study examines only thresholds of 0.7–1.0 on one task. A procedure for choosing these settings without retained-data evaluation or a retrained oracle is not established, weakening the deployment and easy-tuning claims.

Important robustness and reproducibility gaps remain. Component ablations cover only one full-class example, without isolating dynamic reweighting or validating stopping behavior on difficult random-subset tasks. Sequential experiments use fixed five-request sequences with parameters selected per request. Hyperparameters for the random-subset experiments are also absent from Table A7. Broader deletion-set and order variation, together with complete configurations, is needed to substantiate general reliability.
